intro: Hands-on Linux+ labs graded in your browser: simulated RHEL and Ubuntu servers for LVM storage, systemd, accounts and sudo, hardening, disk and network troubleshooting, plus a scripting and automation drill. Changes are checked after a reboot where it matters.

labs.title: Add storage with LVM
labs.summary: Turn a new disk into an LVM volume with an XFS file system, mount it persistently by UUID, prove it survives a reboot, then grow it online.
labs.scenario:
The app server app01 (RHEL) has a new 10 GiB disk, /dev/vdb. The application needs space at /srv/app:

  • Use the whole disk as an LVM physical volume in a volume group vgapp
  • Create a 4 GiB logical volume lvapp with an XFS file system
  • Mount it at /srv/app through /etc/fstab using its UUID
  • Reboot and confirm it's still mounted
  • The app grew faster than planned: extend lvapp and its file system to 6 GiB without unmounting

tasks.text: After a reboot, /srv/app is mounted from lvapp
lvapp and its file system are 6 GiB

hints: Order: pvcreate → vgcreate → lvcreate → mkfs.xfs → mkdir → fstab → mount -a. Run them as root (sudo -i).
blkid /dev/vgapp/lvapp prints the UUID. Edit fstab with vi /etc/fstab, or append with echo ... >> /etc/fstab.
Test fstab with mount -a (and findmnt --verify) before rebooting.
lvextend -r -L 6G grows the volume and the file system together.
labs.solution:
sudo -i
pvcreate /dev/vdb
vgcreate vgapp /dev/vdb
lvcreate -n lvapp -L 4G vgapp
mkfs.xfs /dev/vgapp/lvapp
mkdir /srv/app
blkid /dev/vgapp/lvapp
echo "UUID=<uuid> /srv/app xfs defaults 0 0" >> /etc/fstab
mount -a
reboot
findmnt /srv/app
lvextend -r -L 6G /dev/vgapp/lvapp
df -h /srv/app
labs.review: LVM pools disks into volume groups so logical volumes can grow later. Mount by UUID because device names can change, and always test fstab before a reboot.

labs.title: Fix a failing service
labs.summary: Read systemd status and the journal to find why a service won't start, fix its config, enable it and its timer, and set the default boot target.
labs.scenario: The inventory API on app02 stopped after a config change last night. Get it running and make sure it starts at boot. The nightly report timer, inventory-report.timer, was never turned on. This server also boots to a graphical desktop it doesn't need: make it boot to the multi-user (text) target instead.

requires.msg: inventory: invalid port "80800" in /etc/inventory/inventory.conf: must be 1-65535

journal.msg: inventory: invalid port "80800" in /etc/inventory/inventory.conf: must be 1-65535

tasks.text: Find the error with systemctl status or journalctl
Fix the port: the API should listen on 8081
inventory is running and enabled at boot
Everything still works after a reboot

hints: systemctl status inventory shows recent log lines; journalctl -u inventory shows them all.
Edit the file with sudo vi /etc/inventory/inventory.conf or sudo sed -i 's/80800/8081/' ....
systemctl enable --now enables and starts in one step; it works for timers too.
systemctl set-default multi-user.target
labs.solution:
systemctl status inventory
journalctl -u inventory
sudo sed -i 's/^port=80800/port=8081/' /etc/inventory/inventory.conf
sudo systemctl enable --now inventory
sudo systemctl enable --now inventory-report.timer
sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target
sudo reboot
labs.review: When a unit fails, systemctl status and journalctl -u usually name the problem. Enable controls boot; start controls now. Timers are systemd's alternative to cron.

labs.title: Manage accounts, groups and sudo
labs.summary: Create users and groups, grant a group sudo with a drop-in file, make a service account, and handle account expiry, locking and password aging.
labs.scenario:
Account requests for app03:

  • New group devops with new users dana and omar as members
  • Members of devops can run any command with sudo. Use a file in /etc/sudoers.d/, never edit /etc/sudoers directly
  • omar is a contractor: his account expires on 2026-12-31
  • A system account svc-backup for the backup agent: system UID (below 1000) and no login shell
  • jlee left the company: lock the account but keep the files
  • Passwords of users created from now on must expire after 90 days

tasks.text: svc-backup is a system account with no login shell
jlee is locked and his files are kept
New users' passwords expire after 90 days

hints: useradd -G devops dana adds a supplementary group at creation.
echo '%devops ALL=(ALL) ALL' | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/devops, then check it with sudo visudo -c.
chage -E 2026-12-31 omar; useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin svc-backup; usermod -L jlee.
Password aging defaults for new accounts are in /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS).
labs.solution:
sudo -i
groupadd devops
useradd -G devops dana
useradd -G devops omar
echo '%devops ALL=(ALL) ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/devops
visudo -c
chage -E 2026-12-31 omar
useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin svc-backup
usermod -L jlee
sed -i 's/^PASS_MAX_DAYS.*/PASS_MAX_DAYS	90/' /etc/login.defs
labs.review: Grant privileges to groups, not individuals, and keep sudo rules in drop-in files you can audit and remove. Lock, don't delete, accounts of people who leave until their data is handed over.

labs.title: Harden an internet-facing server
labs.summary: Lock down SSH, remove an insecure service, tighten firewalld, and fix a SUID binary and a world-writable cron file found by find.
labs.scenario:
A security scan of web01 (RHEL) found:

  • SSH allows root logins and passwords. Only key-based logins should work, and never as root
  • The legacy telnet service is running
  • The firewall allows cockpit and port 23/tcp, which aren't needed. HTTPS (the site's only public service besides SSH) isn't allowed. Fix it now and for future boots
  • An unexpected program has the SUID bit set somewhere under /usr/local
  • A file in /etc/cron.d is world-writable

tasks.text: SSH: no root login, no passwords, and sshd restarted
Firewall (runtime and permanent): https allowed; cockpit and 23/tcp removed
The SUID bit is removed from the unexpected program
The cron file is no longer world-writable (mode 644)

hints: Validate sshd config with sudo sshd -t before restarting... in this lab just restart: sudo systemctl restart sshd.
firewall-cmd --permanent changes the saved config; --reload applies it to the running firewall.
find /usr/local -perm -4000 finds SUID files; find /etc/cron.d -perm 666 finds world-writable ones.
labs.solution:
sudo -i
sed -i 's/^PermitRootLogin yes/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sed -i 's/^PasswordAuthentication yes/PasswordAuthentication no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
systemctl restart sshd
systemctl disable --now telnet
firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-service=cockpit --remove-port=23/tcp --add-service=https
firewall-cmd --reload
find /usr/local -perm -4000
chmod u-s /usr/local/bin/netcheck
find /etc/cron.d -perm 666
chmod 644 /etc/cron.d/cleanup
labs.review: Reduce attack surface: key-only SSH without root, no clear-text services, a firewall that allows only what the server offers, and regular scans for SUID and world-writable files.

labs.title: Troubleshoot a full disk and a slow server
labs.summary: Find what filled the root file system with df and du, free space safely, stop a runaway process and lower a backup job's priority.
labs.scenario: ubuntu02 is slow and apps report "No space left on device". Free space on / (target: under 80% used) without breaking the app: the app keeps its log file open, so empty debug.log instead of deleting it. Old crash dumps can go. Also stop the runaway report script hogging the CPU, and make the running rsync backup yield CPU to other work (nice value 10 or higher) without stopping it.

tasks.text: The crash dumps in /var/tmp are deleted
rsync still runs, with a nice value of 10 or more

hints: df -h shows which file system is full; sudo du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h narrows it down.
Empty a file that a program holds open with sudo truncate -s 0 FILE (deleting it wouldn't free the space until the program restarts).
If kill PID doesn't stop a process, kill -9 PID forces it.
sudo renice -n 15 -p PID
labs.solution:
df -h
sudo du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h
sudo du -sh /var/log/app/* /var/tmp/*
sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/app/debug.log
sudo rm /var/tmp/core.*
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head
sudo kill 3150      # ignored
sudo kill -9 3150
sudo renice -n 15 -p 3011
df -h /
labs.review: Work from the top down: df for the file system, du for the directory, then decide what can go. Truncate open logs instead of deleting them, and use nice/renice to shift priority instead of killing work you need.

labs.title: Troubleshoot network connectivity
labs.summary: Find and fix a mistyped IP address, a missing default gateway, the wrong DNS server and a stale /etc/hosts entry, using ip, nmcli, ping and getent.
labs.scenario:
After a hurried rebuild, db01 can't reach anything. It should be:

  • Address 172.25.250.11/24 on connection eth0, with gateway 172.25.250.254
  • DNS server 172.25.250.254 (the internal resolver; public resolvers are blocked)
  • Able to reach repo.example.com (on another network) and utility.lab.example.com by name

Make the fix persistent: it must survive a reboot.

tasks.text: Check the address and routes with ip
Which command shows only the routing table?

hints: Compare ip addr and ip route with what the server should have. nmcli con show eth0 shows the saved settings.
One command fixes all three: sudo nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses ... ipv4.gateway ... ipv4.dns ... ipv4.method manual, then sudo nmcli con up eth0.
getent hosts NAME shows what a name resolves to; /etc/hosts wins over DNS.
labs.solution:
ip addr
ip route
nmcli con show eth0
sudo nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 172.25.250.11/24 ipv4.gateway 172.25.250.254 ipv4.dns 172.25.250.254 ipv4.method manual
sudo nmcli con up eth0
getent hosts utility.lab.example.com
sudo sed -i '/utility/d' /etc/hosts
ping -c 3 repo.example.com
sudo reboot
ping -c 3 repo.example.com
labs.review: Work up the stack: address and mask, then gateway (can you leave the subnet?), then name resolution (/etc/hosts before DNS). nmcli changes are saved in the connection profile, so they survive a reboot.

labs.title: Scripting, Git and automation
labs.summary: Complete a Bash script, put a Git workflow in order, and match Ansible and infrastructure-as-code terms.
labs.scenario: You're automating user onboarding: a Bash script now, then an Ansible playbook in a Git repository.

activities.title: Finish the script
activities.prompt:
This script creates every user named on the command line and refuses to run without arguments. Fill in the blanks. 
____ (1)
set -euo pipefail
if [ ____ (2) -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "usage: $0 USER..." >&2
  exit 1
fi
for u in ____ (3); do
  useradd "$u"
done

rows.label: (3) all arguments, each as its own word

activities.title: Git workflow
activities.prompt: Put the steps for changing a playbook in order.
items: Open a pull request for review

activities.title: Automation terms
activities.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

items.text: The list of hosts and groups Ansible manages
A YAML file of plays and tasks
A unit of work such as dnf, user or copy
Running it again changes nothing if the system is already correct
Servers and settings defined in version-controlled files

hints: $# is the argument count; "$@" keeps each argument separate even if it contains spaces.
labs.review: Scripts automate one machine; Ansible applies the same desired state to many, idempotently. Git adds history and review to both.

labs.title: Break it, then fix it: a web page that returns 403
labs.summary: Deliberately mislabel a web page, watch it fail with a 403 even though the permissions are fine, find the SELinux cause and repair it the right way.
labs.scenario:
servera serves a company page from /var/www/html and SELinux is enforcing. In this lab you will break it first, so you learn what the failure looks like, then fix it without turning SELinux off.

  1. Check the page works: curl http://localhost
  2. Break it: sudo chcon -t user_home_t /var/www/html/index.html (this mimics a file copied in from a home directory)
  3. Request the page again and read the error
  4. Find why: ls -Z and ls -l on the file
  5. Fix it the right way and verify

tasks.text: Confirm the page works before you break it (curl http://localhost)
Look at the file's SELinux label (ls -Z)
Fix it with restorecon and keep SELinux enforcing
Verify: the page loads from other machines (HTTP 200)

questions.prompt: The file permissions are fine (644) and httpd is running. Why is the page forbidden?
options: The file's SELinux type is not one httpd may read
The file is owned by the wrong user

hints: ls -lZ /var/www/html/index.html shows both the permissions and the SELinux type.
The type httpd expects for web content is httpd_sys_content_t.
sudo restorecon -v /var/www/html/index.html resets the label from the policy; don't use setenforce 0.
labs.solution:
curl http://localhost
sudo chcon -t user_home_t /var/www/html/index.html
curl -I http://localhost      # 403 Forbidden
ls -lZ /var/www/html/index.html
sudo restorecon -v /var/www/html/index.html
curl http://localhost
labs.review: A 403 with correct Unix permissions and a running service is the classic SELinux signature. Files copied or moved from a home directory keep user_home_t; restorecon puts back the label the policy defines. Setting SELinux to permissive hides the symptom without fixing it.
